extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and scholars of literature, critics and adaptors interested in Vladimir Nabokov's Lolita
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and descriptive criteria for reading, interpreting, and adapting Vladimir Nabokov's novel Lolita, focusing on intertextuality, authorial stance, provenance/prototype issues, translation, and adaptation choices. Useful for critics, teachers, and adaptors assessing the novel's techniques and legacies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of allusions to classical and modern literature
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel abounds in allusions to classical and modern literature; virtually all of them have been noted in The Annotated Lolita, and many are references to Humbert's own favorite poet, Edgar Allan Poe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include the naming of Annabel Leigh after Poe's 'Annabel Lee', verbatim reuse of Poe's phrases (e.g., chapter 11 quote), and reprise of Poe-like lines in chapter openings. Evaluate frequency, explicitness (verbatim vs. oblique), and how the allusions deepen character or theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pastiche and parody as deliberate stylistic devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Nabokov uses pastiche and parody (e.g., opening is a pastiche of Poe; chapter 26 contains a parody of Joyce's stream-of-consciousness; chapter 35 parodies the rhythm/anaphora of T. S. Eliot).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how effective mimicry/parody is at creating ironic distance, commentary, or aesthetic effects. Note which author/style is being echoed and whether the pastiche functions as homage, critique, or formal experimentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming and doubling (doppelgänger motif)
rubrics_metrics.description: Names and naming (e.g., 'Humbert Humbert' double name) recall other works ('William Wilson') and signal motifs such as the doppelgänger, paralleling characters like Clare Quilty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider names as deliberate intertextual signals that encode thematic parallels (identity split, alter ego). Evaluate whether naming functions symbolically, ironically, or as structural device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrator's scholarly expertise informs intertextual references
rubrics_metrics.description: Humbert's field of expertise (French literature) grounds references to Flaubert, Proust, Rabelais, Baudelaire, Balzac, etc., integrating learned commentary into the narration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge how convincingly the narrator's erudition justifies literary allusions and whether those references shape reader perception of reliability, authority, or bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtlety versus direct allusion (strategic avoidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although Nabokov loved Lewis Carroll and translated Alice in Wonderland, he avoided direct allusions to Carroll in Lolita, preferring brief or oblique references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the aesthetic or ethical effects of subtle versus overt allusion; assess when restraint strengthens ambiguity or when explicit referencing would be more clarifying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of real-life prototypes and source material
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel may draw on real-life cases and predecessors (e.g., possible links to Charlie Chaplin/Lita Grey, Florence Horner/Frank La Salle, Nabokov's earlier The Enchanter), and Nabokov even mentions the Horner case in the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing origin/influence, weigh documentary parallels, authorial acknowledgement, and fictional transformation. Consider ethical implications of fictionalizing traumatic real events and how closely to credit sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing influence from plagiarism (cryptomnesia debates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholars debate the discovery of a 1916 German short story 'Lolita' and whether Nabokov might have had cryptomnesia; commentators (e.g., Maar) raised the issue while others argue plagiarism should not apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use criteria such as originality of plot/detail, uniqueness of admired elements, and whether the later work is 'deducible' from the earlier; evaluate claims against the larger literary practice of reworking themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial stance on didacticism and moralizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Nabokov asserts that 'Lolita has no moral in tow' and that a work of fiction exists insofar as it affords 'aesthetic bliss' rather than serving didactic purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique and evaluation should account for Nabokov's declared aesthetic aims: prioritize language, form, and aesthetic effect over moral lessons when judging the novel's success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language choice and translation sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Nabokov's relationship with language (abandoning Russian for English; the Russian translation's Postscriptum and retention of the American afterword) affects textual voice and reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess translations and bilingual editions for how they preserve or alter tone, voice, and authorial commentary; consider authorial remarks about language when judging diction and idiom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation decisions: fidelity and alteration (age, character emphasis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adaptations often alter elements (e.g., Kubrick's film raises Lolita's age to 14 and expands Quilty), reflecting medium constraints, censorship, or interpretive choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating adaptations, note what is changed (age, plot beats, character focus), why (legal, ethical, commercial, artistic), and how changes affect themes and reader/viewer reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staging and representation of sexual content (ethical/aesthetic balance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some adaptations (stage/film) have been criticized for staging that appears to normalize or misplace blame for sexual abuse; choices in depiction strongly affect audience interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique staging choices for whether they foreground victimhood, excuse or eroticize abuse, or responsibly contextualize harm. Use contemporary ethical standards alongside artistic aims when assessing such portrayals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perspective-shifts (narrator-centered vs victim-centered retellings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivative works and adaptations sometimes shift point of view (e.g., Lo's Diary retells from Lolita's POV; one-man plays center Humbert), which fundamentally alters interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how changing perspective reassigns narrative authority and ethical weight: does it restore a silenced voice, complicate culpability, or merely reframe the original?

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermedial transformation and medium-specific emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel has been adapted across media (film, musical, opera, ballet, screenplay, radio), with each medium emphasizing different elements (music, movement, visual spectacle, internal monologue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess adaptations by how well they translate novelistic devices (unreliable narration, verbal play, intertextuality) into medium-specific techniques (score, choreography, visual motif) and whether the adaptation's emphasis serves or distorts core themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody and derivative works as critical commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Parodies and retellings (e.g., Umberto Eco's 'Granita', Jean Kerr's piece, Steve Martin's 'Lolita at Fifty') use imitation or inversion to comment on, critique, or extend Nabokov's novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging such works, consider whether parody illuminates the source, satirizes cultural reception, or offers meaningful reinterpretation versus mere pastiche.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural reception and semantic shift of 'Lolita'
rubrics_metrics.description: The name 'Lolita' has shifted in contemporary usage from the novel's victim to a term for a 'precociously seductive girl', reflecting cultural appropriation and semantic drift.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critiques should account for how reception history changes interpretive frameworks; consider the social consequences of semantic shifts when discussing cultural impact and ethics.
